 Delta says US air traffic control is holding back route efficiency
 Published on November 15, 2026 | Translated from Spanish 
 Category: Motoring and automotive › Mobility and public transport 
 Delta CEO Ed Bastian has put an uncomfortable reality on the table for American aviation: air traffic control management means some commercial routes now take longer than they did in the 1950s. He cited the Atlanta-LaGuardia route as an example, whose current duration exceeds that of decades ago due to infrastructure that isn't keeping pace with the industry.
 1960s radars and a shortfall of 3,500 professionals ✈️
 Air traffic controllers continue working with radar systems designed in the 1960s and screens that have already outlived their useful life. On top of this, the FAA is carrying a shortfall of some 3,500 professionals, which strains daily operations. The administration announced a plan to upgrade more than 4,600 facilities with satellite and GPS technologies, although its cost ranges between $12.5 billion and $50 billion and funding has yet to be secured.
 Modernizing the sky, that unfinished business since the last century 🛰️
 The good news is that there is already a plan to upgrade 4,600 facilities. The bad news is that no one can quite decide who puts up the $50 billion. Meanwhile, passengers can console themselves by thinking that their Atlanta-LaGuardia flight is almost a vintage experience: same duration as in the fifties, but with onboard wifi. Quite the retro luxury.
